prompt: A 1,024-node cluster uses push gossip with fanout 1 per second. Assume synchronous rounds, reliable delivery, independent uniform peer choices on a complete graph and one initially informed node. Using the asymptotic leading-term estimate, roughly how long until a new membership change reaches (almost) every node?

options.explanation: Wrong. That's linear spread (one new node per round). Gossip spreads exponentially because every informed node also gossips.
Wrong. In one round, only one more node learns it; it can't reach 1,024 nodes in a single exchange with fanout 1.

Correct. The informed set roughly doubles each round at first (1,024 is 2 doubled 10 times), but random peer choice makes the last few nodes slow to reach. Push gossip needs about 17 rounds for 1,024 nodes.

options.text: It never converges without a central server.
options.explanation: Wrong. Gossip is specifically designed to converge without a coordinator.

workedExample:
Each round, every informed node tells one random peer.

| Round | Informed (ideal) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 10 | ~1,024 |

That doubling is the best case. As more nodes know, more pushes land on nodes that already know, so the final stragglers take extra rounds. For push gossip, the leading terms of the asymptotic expected total are (the constant and practical effects are omitted):

```formula
r ≈ log_2(N) + ln(N)
r ≈ log_2(1,024) + ln(1,024)
r ≈ 10 + 6.9 ≈ 17
where
r: rounds until every node knows; at one round per second, also the time in seconds
N: the number of nodes; here 1,024
log_2: base-2 logarithm: how many doublings get from 1 to N
ln: natural logarithm (base e ≈ 2.718)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: about 10 rounds of doubling, plus about 7 more to reach the last stragglers, so roughly 17 seconds.
```

Push-pull shortens the tail. Each informed node initiates one contact per second. Incoming contacts fluctuate, and message bytes depend on state size; this is not a constant-bandwidth guarantee.
